relationship: women and children explicitly included in the assembly before the Lord
rationale: Chronicles explicitly includes children and women as all Judah stands before the Lord; Deuteronomy calls for Israel to appear before Him and commands the gathering of men, women, children and the sojourner. The correspondence concerns the assembly's inclusive composition; Chronicles' crisis prayer is not identified as the prescribed festival reading.

relationship: women and children present within the whole assembled people
rationale: Chronicles names the children and women standing with all Judah; the native Joshua continuation unit names women and children among the whole assembly hearing the law. Both explicitly include these family members, while the prayer assembly and law reading remain distinct events and Joshua's original 9:2f reference is preserved.

relationship: royal agricultural works combining water provision, cultivated land and livestock
rationale: Uzziah's works include cisterns, herds and vinedressers, with his love of farming stated; the royal speaker in Ecclesiastes describes vineyards, gardens, water pools and great herds and flocks. The shared combination gives a particular parallel in royal agriculture, without equating the rulers or the cisterns for herds with the pools used to irrigate trees.

relationship: gifts brought to the Lord after His victory over hostile power
rationale: Chronicles places gifts to the Lord at Jerusalem after the defeat of Assyria and Jerusalem's deliverance; Psalm 75, explicitly titled concerning the Assyrian, moves from God's defeat of weapons at Zion to gifts brought to the Lord who overawes rulers. The link concerns the gifts to God after divine victory, not a claim that the psalm names Hezekiah or records the separate presents to him.

relationship: royal provision for produce stores and livestock
rationale: Hezekiah's possessions include provision for grain, oil and wine and places for animals and flocks; David's estate roster separately names storehouses, wine and oil stores, cattle and sheep. The detailed combination connects the management of royal agricultural resources while preserving the different rulers, personnel and types of facilities.

relationship: same-book accounts of separate royal wall works naming Ophla
rationale: Manasseh's wall account names a course toward Ophla; Jotham's account explicitly names building on the wall of Ophla. This narrow named-place correspondence connects two periods of fortification work without claiming that the whole wall, gate, Gihon route or construction phase is identical.
